topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the Same World through Different Eyes

outline.topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the Same World through Different Eyes

sections.title: The Hook: The Tale of Two Navigators
sections.content: Introduce a scenario where two characters, Alice and Bob, are navigating the same terrain but using different maps. Alice uses a standard North-East grid (Standard Basis), while Bob uses a grid aligned with a tilted mountain range (Basis B). Establish that they are looking at the same 'Point P' but have different coordinates for it.
sections.example: Alice says the treasure is at (3, 2). Bob, standing on his tilted grid, says it's at (1, 1). Who is right? Both are! They are just using different 'languages' or bases.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: What is a Basis?
sections.content: Briefly define a basis as a set of 'unit' vectors that act as building blocks. In 2D, any point can be reached by a combination of two non-parallel vectors. Visualize the standard basis i (1,0) and j (0,1) as a clean square grid.
sections.example: Animation: Show a vector [3, 2] being constructed by 3 steps of i and 2 steps of j. Then, swap the grid to two diagonal arrows to show a new 'custom' grid being formed.

sections.title: The Translation Matrix (The 'Dictionary')
sections.content: Explain that to understand Bob, Alice needs to know what Bob's basic 'steps' (basis vectors b1 and b2) look like in her world. We arrange Bob's basis vectors as columns in a matrix. This matrix P is our 'Dictionary' or Change of Basis Matrix.
sections.example: If Bob's first step b1 looks like (2, 1) to Alice, and his second step b2 looks like (-1, 1) to Alice, the matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]].

sections.title: The Core Formula: Mapping Coordinates
sections.content: Present the fundamental equation: [v]_Alice = P * [v]_Bob. Explain that multiplying Bob's coordinates by matrix P 'translates' them into Alice's standard coordinate system. Use a visual of Bob's grid morphing and stretching to align with Alice's square grid.
sections.example: If Bob says a bird is at (1, 1) in his system, Alice calculates: [[2, -1], [1, 1]] * [1, 1]^T = [1, 2]. Alice sees the bird at (1, 2) in her standard system.

sections.title: Going Backwards: The Inverse Matrix
sections.content: What if Alice wants to tell Bob where the bird is? We need the Inverse Matrix (P^-1). Explain that [v]_Bob = P^-1 * [v]_Alice. This allows for two-way communication between different viewpoints.
sections.example: Alice sees a cloud at (4, 2). By multiplying by the inverse of P, she can tell Bob exactly where to look on his tilted map.

sections.title: Visual Summary and Application
sections.content: Summarize that a Change of Basis is simply a linear transformation that reinterprets coordinates. Mention real-world applications like computer graphics (camera vs. world space) or JPEG compression (pixel space vs. frequency space).
sections.example: Animation: A 3D camera moving through a forest. As the camera (Bob) rotates, the trees (Points) stay the same in the world (Alice), but their coordinates relative to the camera change constantly via basis transformation.

storyboard.title: The Hook: The Tale of Two Navigators
lecture_lines: Meet Alice and Bob exploring the same terrain.
Alice uses a standard North-East grid map.
Bob's map aligns with the tilted mountain range.
They see the same treasure at different coordinates.
Both are correct, using different basis languages.
animations: Display a standard white grid labeled "Alice's Grid" with white axes.
Overlay a tilted blue (#0000FF) grid labeled "Bob's Grid" on the screen.
Mark a single red (#FF0000) point 'P' that exists on both grids.
Show coordinates (3, 2) in white next to Point P on Alice's grid.
Show coordinates (1, 1) in blue (#0000FF) next to Point P on Bob's grid.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Check: What is a Basis?
lecture_lines: A basis is a set of unit building blocks.
The standard basis i and j form squares.
Any two non-parallel vectors can form a basis.
animations: Show unit vectors i=(1,0) in red (#FF0000) and j=(0,1) in green (#00FF00).
Create a full white square grid by repeating i and j vectors.
Change i and j to diagonal vectors (2,1) and (-1,1) and skew grid.

storyboard.title: The Translation Matrix (The 'Dictionary')
lecture_lines: Alice needs to understand Bob's unique steps.
Bob's basis vectors are columns in a matrix.
This matrix P acts as a translation dictionary.
animations: Display vectors b1=(2,1) and b2=(-1,1) in Alice's standard white grid.
Morph b1 and b2 into columns of matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]].
Flash matrix P in yellow (#FFFF00) and label it "Dictionary".

storyboard.title: The Core Formula: Mapping Coordinates
lecture_lines: The formula maps Bob's coordinates to Alice's.
Multiplying by P translates Bob's view to Alice's.
Bob's grid morphs to align with Alice's system.
Calculation confirms the point's position in Alice's grid.
The transformation links their two different perspectives.
animations: Write formula [v]_Alice = P * [v]_Bob in white (#FFFFFF) at top.
Show matrix P multiplying a generic vector [v]_Bob.
Animate Bob's grid morphing and stretching into Alice's square grid.
Plug in Bob's coordinates (1, 1) into the formula on screen.
Show result (1, 2) and highlight point on the Alice grid.

storyboard.title: Going Backwards: The Inverse Matrix
lecture_lines: To speak Bob's language, use the inverse matrix.
The inverse P reverses the coordinate translation process.
Now Alice can describe points for Bob's map.
animations: Show Alice's point (4, 2) on her standard white grid.
Introduce the inverse matrix P^-1 in cyan (#00FFFF) next to point.
Apply P^-1 to (4, 2) and show point on Bob's blue grid.

storyboard.title: Visual Summary and Application
lecture_lines: Change of basis reinterprets the same vector.
Matrix P and its inverse enable two-way communication.
This is essential for modern computer graphics.
JPEG compression uses this to store images efficiently.
Different bases offer unique insights into the world.
animations: Show a 2D camera icon rotating to represent changing viewpoints.
Show a grid relative to camera rotating while world objects stay fixed.
Display text "Computer Graphics" in cyan (#00FFFF).
Display text "JPEG Compression" in magenta (#FF00FF).
Fade out and show the core formula one last time in white.
